pedagogy.summary: At age 9-10 children read and complete real information tables — bus and train timetables and two-way tables (e.g. favourite sport by gender) — and solve one- and two-step problems from them: find a departure time, work out a journey duration, complete a missing cell, compare two values. Two things carry the teaching. First, tracking a value to the intersection of the correct ROW and COLUMN, because dense timetables invite off-by-one-row/column reading. Second, and most characteristically, computing time DURATIONS correctly: children who read '10:50' and '11:20' tend to subtract the digits as if time were decimal (getting 0.70, or calling a 2:23 journey 'two point two three hours'), because minutes are base-60, not base-10. The remedy is to count on in minutes across the hour on a clock or number line, never to subtract clock readings as decimals. Keep every table anchored in a real purpose (catch the bus, plan the journey) so the numbers mean something.
bestPractices: Track every value to the ROW×COLUMN intersection explicitly — finger on the row, finger on the column, meet in the middle — to defeat off-by-one-row/column reading in dense timetables

Teach durations by COUNTING ON in minutes across the hour (10:50 → 11:00 is 10 min, → 11:20 is another 20, so 30 min), using an empty number line or clock face — never by subtracting clock readings as if decimals

Confront the time-as-decimal habit head-on: when a child says a journey takes 0.70 or 2.23 hours, use an analogue clock to show 60 minutes in an hour so the digits after the colon are seen as minutes, not tenths
Underline the question words ('how long', 'how many more', 'how much later') so children compute the DIFFERENCE/DURATION asked for rather than reading a single value off the table
Read two-way tables by naming what each cell, row total and column total MEANS ('this cell is girls who chose football; this end number is all the girls') before doing any arithmetic
Anchor tables in an authentic task — catch the 8:40 bus, work out if you make the connection — so reading is purposeful rather than mechanical
keyRepresentations: A real bus/train timetable grid (services in columns, stops in rows) — the canonical structure for this age
A two-way table (e.g. sport × gender) with row and column totals shown
An empty number line or clock face for counting on the minutes of a duration across the hour
A finger/ruler trace from row and column to their intersection cell
commonMisconceptions: Reading time as a decimal number: giving a journey duration as 0.70 or '2.23 hours' by subtracting or reading clock digits as base-10 rather than counting minutes in base-60
Reading off a single value when a difference or duration is asked ('how many more', 'how much longer') instead of computing it
Off-by-one-row/column reading: taking the value from an adjacent service or stop in a dense grid
In a two-way table, confusing a row/column TOTAL (a margin) with a single cell, or double-counting when categories overlap

learn.summary: For ages 9-10, teach children to read and complete real information tables — bus/train timetables and two-way tables (e.g. favourite sport by gender) — and to solve one- and two-step problems: find a departure time, compute a journey duration, complete a missing cell, compare two values. Two difficulties carry the teaching: tracking a value to the correct ROW×COLUMN intersection (dense grids invite off-by-one reading), and computing time DURATIONS by counting on in minutes across the hour rather than subtracting clock readings as if they were base-10 decimals. Keep every table anchored in an authentic purpose (catch the bus, plan the journey) so the numbers mean something.

activities.title: Live timetable with intersection highlighting
feedback: If the answer belongs to a neighbouring row or column, re-trace: one finger on the row, one on the column, and read only where they meet; use a ruler edge to isolate the row in a crowded timetable.
If a duration comes out as 0.70 or '70', re-count the jumps: to the next o'clock first (10:50→11:00 = 10 min), then past it (→11:20 = 20 min), total 30 minutes.

If the answer is only slightly out (e.g. a jump miscounted, or a boundary minute counted twice when counting minute by minute), the counting-on approach is likely sound — have them re-mark the jumps on a number line and re-add rather than reteaching the concept.
activities.rationale: Tracking to the intersection and counting minutes in base-60 are the two hardest parts of this skill, and making them felt through tracing and counting-on targets the specific off-by-one and time-as-decimal errors. Optional live highlighting and a minute-track are concrete ways to make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Children read digital/clock times as decimal numbers: from a bus timetable they compute a journey as '2.23' and say it takes 'two point two three hours', interpreting the digits after the point as a decimal fraction rather than minutes; the remedy is an analogue clock and discussing how many minutes are in an hour
learnerActions: Use a real bus/train timetable (often services in columns and stops in rows, but check the headings because layouts vary) to find when a named service reaches a named stop.

Track the stop-row with one finger and the service-column with the other, meeting at the intersecting cell. If a screen model is available, tapping a row and column can light up ONLY the intersecting cell so the off-by-one habit has nowhere to hide.

Find a journey duration by counting on in minutes across the hour: 10:50 → 11:00 is 10 minutes, → 11:20 is another 20, so 30 minutes. If a duration tool is available, drag a marker along a minute-track and watch it tick across the hour.
State out loud why you cannot simply subtract 11:20 − 10:50 and call it 0.70 — the digits after the colon are minutes out of 60, not tenths of an hour.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading tables is a doing skill on a 2D grid: values live at a row×column intersection, and time durations are counted in minutes across the hour, not subtracted as decimals.

activities.title: Confront time-as-decimal with an analogue clock
feedback: If the child still subtracts digits, return to the clock: show the 60 minutes in the hour and count the jumps to and past the o'clock.
Check the 14:45 + 40 min answer: 14:45→15:00 is 15 min, then 25 more to 15:25.
Check the 'next service 25 minutes later' answer: from 10:50, count 10:50→11:00 is 10 min, then 15 more to 11:15, so it leaves at 11:15.
activities.rationale: The source names reading clock times as decimals as a known misconception and names the analogue clock plus 'how many minutes in an hour' as the remedy, so this activity confronts the habit directly and rehearses it across the hour in both directions.
sourceClaims: Children read digital/clock times as decimal numbers: from a bus timetable they compute a journey as '2.23' and say it takes 'two point two three hours', interpreting the digits after the point as a decimal fraction rather than minutes; the remedy is an analogue clock and discussing how many minutes are in an hour
learnerActions: When a journey duration has been found by subtracting clock times as if they were decimals (e.g. 11:20 − 10:50 written as 0.70, or '70 minutes'), look at an analogue clock and state how many minutes are in one hour (60).
Find the correct duration in minutes by counting on from the start time to the end time across the hour on the clock face or an empty number line (e.g. 10:50 → 11:00 → 11:20 = 30 minutes).
Try a journey that crosses the hour in the other direction too — e.g. a train leaving at 14:45 with a 40-minute journey: when does it arrive?
Combine a lookup with a forward duration: if the next service is 25 minutes later than the one shown (say it leaves at 10:50), count on to find its departure time rather than adding digits.
activities.intendedInsight: The digits after the colon are minutes out of 60, not tenths of an hour, so durations must be counted in minutes, not read as decimals.

activities.title: Complete and interpret a two-way table
feedback: If the child reports a single cell (e.g. the number of girls who chose football) when a difference was asked, re-read the underlined 'how many MORE' and point to both values before subtracting.

If a margin total is confused with a single cell, name each number's meaning again before arithmetic. (In a sport-by-gender table the categories do not overlap; keep the double-counting caution for tables where a child could be counted in more than one category.)
activities.rationale: The source names reading off a single value when a difference is asked as a misconception, with underlining the question words as the remedy; naming cells vs totals first targets margin-vs-cell confusion.
sourceClaims: When asked 'how many more' from a chart/table, children read off a single value (e.g. the number one child has) instead of computing the difference; underlining the question words 'how many more' helps direct attention to the required operation
learnerActions: Before any arithmetic, name what each cell, row total and column total MEANS (e.g. 'this cell is girls who chose football; this end number is all the girls').

Complete a missing cell in a two-way table of favourite sport by gender from the given data, checking the filled cell against its row and column totals. If a screen model is available, row and column totals can update live so a filled cell can be checked against its margins.
Answer a 'how many more' question — underline the question words, point to BOTH values, and show the subtraction.
Contrast with a plain 'how many' question so the difference between reading one value and computing a difference is explicit.
activities.intendedInsight: A cell, a row total and a column total mean different things; 'how many more' asks for a difference between two values, not a single read-off.

activities.title: Scorable checks on lookups, durations and cell completion
feedback: A cross-the-hour duration item surfaces decimal subtraction (0.70/'70') versus a correct 30 minutes — if wrong, return to counting on across the hour.
A 'how many more' item surfaces reading a single value instead of a difference — if wrong, point to both values and subtract.
activities.rationale: Lookups, durations and complete-the-cell tasks give a scorable check of the reading procedure; purposely including a cross-the-hour duration and a 'how many more' item catches the two named misconceptions. This format checks a recognition/completion response and does not by itself elicit the child's independent counting-on method, so pair it with the watched performance task.
sourceClaims: Children read digital/clock times as decimal numbers: from a bus timetable they compute a journey as '2.23' and say it takes 'two point two three hours', interpreting the digits after the point as a decimal fraction rather than minutes; the remedy is an analogue clock and discussing how many minutes are in an hour

When asked 'how many more' from a chart/table, children read off a single value (e.g. the number one child has) instead of computing the difference; underlining the question words 'how many more' helps direct attention to the required operation
learnerActions: Find a departure time from a shown timetable (selecting from options).
Complete 'the journey from A to B takes ___ minutes', including at least one item where the arrival crosses the hour (e.g. 10:50→11:20).
Complete or fill a missing cell in a two-way table.
Answer one 'how many more' item that requires a difference, not a single value.
activities.intendedInsight: The reading-and-calculating procedure can be checked against items deliberately chosen to catch time-as-decimal and read-off-instead-of-difference errors.

activities.title: Annotated worked-example timetable (scaffold)
feedback: Once the parts are named confidently, move to a table the child completes and calculates on themselves — this annotated example lets the child recognise structure but does not itself let them perform a duration calculation or complete a table.
activities.rationale: A static annotated grid can label structure and reveal what a cell means, which is a useful orientation, but it pre-bakes answers and does not elicit the duration or completion skill. It is a worked example only, not a substitute for the child doing the calculation.
learnerActions: Study a labelled timetable grid where the structure is annotated: services vs stops and what a single time cell means (and, on a two-way table, a single cell vs a row or column total), with tap-to-reveal explanations of what each part means.
Use it to rehearse naming the parts before doing your own lookups and durations on a live table.
activities.intendedInsight: Understanding the grid structure (services, stops and cells in a timetable; cells and totals in a two-way table) supports accurate reading before the child performs lookups and duration calculations independently.

constraints: Durations must be taught by counting on in minutes across the hour (to the o'clock, then past it) on a clock face or empty number line — never by subtracting clock readings as if they were base-10 decimals.

A static annotated/tap-to-reveal timetable is a worked example only: it orients the child to structure but does not itself let them perform a duration calculation or complete a table, which are the actual skills.
Scorable multiple-choice/fill items check recognition and completion and do not by themselves elicit the child's independent counting-on method; pair them with a watched performance task.
Keep every table anchored in an authentic purpose (catch the bus, make the connection) so reading is meaningful rather than mechanical.
Prerequisites may need reteaching: time conversion/minutes-in-an-hour for duration errors, and careful grid reading for off-by-one-row/column errors.
The double-counting caution applies only to tables where a child could fall into more than one category; a mutually-exclusive table (e.g. sport by gender) does not overlap.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row ranked a conversational format and a third spatial dimension as poor fit for this flat-grid skill and described them as 'adds nothing'. They are dropped rather than asserted as universal pedagogical laws, since the catalog ranking does not establish comparative efficacy or necessity; a flat grid simply does not require a third spatial dimension for this content.

Arithmetic check: 10:50→11:00 = 10 min, →11:20 = 20 min, total 30 min (correct); 14:45 + 40 min = 15:25 (correct); 10:50 + 25 min = 11:15 (correct). The erroneous '0.70'/'70' results are retained only as the misconception to confront, never as valid answers.
Efficacy of optional live-highlight and minute-track interactions is not source-established; they are offered with 'if available'/'may help' wording.

The Year 5 curriculum source claim establishes that completing/reading/interpreting tables is appropriate content for this age but does not evidence any individual activity's mechanism rationale, so it is not cited within the activities; its placement support is reflected in the summary context only.

probeDeeper: 'The bus leaves at 10:50 and arrives at 11:20 — show me how you worked out the 30 minutes.' — forces the method into the open
'A train leaves at 14:45 and the journey is 40 minutes — when does it arrive?' — transfer across the hour in the other direction
'What does this number at the end of the row mean?' (a row total) — probes cell-vs-total understanding
'If the next bus is 25 minutes later than this one, what time does it leave?' — combines reading with a duration in a fresh direction
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: for (1) the child tracks the correct row and column to their intersection and reads the right time; for (2) they compute the duration by counting on in minutes across the hour (10:50→11:20 = 30 minutes), not by subtracting the digits; for (3) they complete the cell using the right row and column (checking against a total if available) and give the DIFFERENCE between girls and boys, not a single value. Tracking to the intersection and counting minutes in base-60 are the marks of mastery.

errorPatterns.pattern: Time-as-decimal: computes a duration by subtracting or reading clock times as base-10 numbers — giving 0.70 for 10:50 to 11:20, or calling a journey '2.23 hours' — because minutes are treated as tenths rather than sixtieths
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach duration on the time-conversion prerequisite: use an analogue clock and empty number line, establish 60 minutes in an hour, and count on 10:50→11:00→11:20 so the child sees the answer as minutes, not tenths
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) the child subtracts the digits (11:20 − 10:50 → '70' or '0.70'/'0.30') or reports the duration as a decimal number of hours, rather than counting minutes across the hour

errorPatterns.pattern: Read-off-instead-of-difference: when asked 'how many more' or 'how much longer', reads a single value straight off the table rather than computing the difference between two
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront in place: underline the question words 'how many MORE', and have the child point to BOTH values and show the subtraction; contrast with a plain 'how many' question to make the difference explicit
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the 'how many more girls than boys' part of task (3), the child states the number of girls who chose football (a single cell) instead of subtracting the boys' value

errorPatterns.pattern: Off-by-one-row/column reading: in a dense grid, takes the value from an adjacent service or stop — the correct kind of value but from the wrong intersection
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach careful grid reading on the tables prerequisite: track the row with one finger and the column with the other and meet at the intersection; use a ruler/edge to isolate the row in a crowded timetable
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (1) the child gives a plausible but wrong time that belongs to the neighbouring column/row, without tracking row and column to their meeting point

errorPatterns.pattern: Counting-on slip: uses the right count-on method for a duration but miscounts the minutes (e.g. counts the hour boundary twice), giving an answer a few minutes out
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: have them re-mark the jumps on the number line (to the o'clock, then past it) and re-add; the concept is intact, only the count slipped
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) the child's method is sound — counting on across the hour — but the total is off by a few minutes

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably find a departure time (reads the wrong row/column), and computes durations by treating clock times as decimals
responseLevels.full: Tracks values to the correct row×column intersection, computes durations by counting on in minutes across the hour, finds differences, completes and uses two-way table totals, and transfers the same reading to a fresh timetable unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Reads individual departure times and completes given cells correctly, but computes durations by decimal subtraction, or reads off a single value when a difference/duration is asked — reads the data but not between it

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a real bus or train timetable (services in columns, several stops in rows) and a partly-completed two-way table (e.g. favourite sport by gender, with some cells and one total missing) in front of the child. Set these tasks and WATCH how they do them, saying little: (1) 'Find the time the 9:15 service reaches [named stop].' (2) 'How long does the journey from [stop A] to [stop B] take on that service?' — choose stops where the arrival crosses the hour (e.g. 10:50 to 11:20). (3) 'Fill in the missing cell in this table, and tell me how many MORE girls than boys chose football.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not model the duration method or point to the right cell.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Task (2) is chosen to cross the hour, so a child treating time as decimal produces a visibly wrong duration (0.70, or '70') while a child counting on gives 30 minutes — the two reason to different answers on the same question. Task (3) pairs a straight lookup with a 'how many more', separating a child who reads the data from one who reads between it; and the two-way structure exposes row/column-total confusion that a single lookup would hide.
